## Recommendation

Cleaning the hulls and recovering kernels before selling to the local dairy ranks first. It has an expected net of $98 per ton, or $98,000 for the 1,000-ton lot. That is $13 per ton ($13,000) more than the baseline, selling to the local dairy as-is, at $85 per ton ($85,000).

Treat this as a lean, not a firm call. The edge depends on placeholder values for cleaning cost ($10 per ton) and recovered kernel value ($20–$26 per ton). Get an equipment or toll-cleaning quote first. If you can't, selling to the local dairy is the safe fallback.

Aflatoxin has not been tested, and that applies to every feed or food route. Test before selling anything.

## How the options compare

| Option | Expected net per ton | Expected total | vs. baseline per ton |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clean, recover kernels, sell to dairy | $98 | $98,000 | +$13 |
| Local dairy (baseline) | $85 | $85,000 | – |
| Distant dairy | $56 | $56,000 | -$29 |
| Bioenergy | $17 | $17,000 | -$68 |
| Compost or soil | $16 | $16,000 | -$69 |
| Hull powder food ingredient | needs quote | – | – |

- The dairy price range of $76–$106 per ton is sourced [giannini2026]. The hauling rate is also sourced. Mileage is a placeholder.
- The clean-and-recover option uses the same dairy price as the baseline. Its gain comes only from kernel value, less cleaning cost.
- The distant dairy pays more per ton ($116–$146), but that price is a placeholder, and $75 per ton of freight eats the premium. It would need about $160 per ton to match the baseline.
- Bioenergy and compost are far behind, and all their values are placeholders. They would need about $103 and $99 per ton to match the baseline.
- The food ingredient has no public price [gras2026], so it can't be recommended. A buyer would need to quote about $175 per ton to match the baseline.

## What could change the answer

- **Kernel value and cleaning cost.** Both are placeholders. Recoverable kernel is about 1–1.3% of hull-pile weight [abc_food2025], but recovered kernels may grade lower.
- **Dairy price swings.** Prices have gone from about $60 per ton to $130 [farmprogress_low, wcngg2022]. The baseline's own range is $70–$100 net per ton. The clean-and-recover range is $80–$116, so the two ranges overlap.
- **Buyer leverage.** About 97% of hulls already go to dairy rations [farmprogress_low], so local buyers hold bargaining power.
- **Real distances.** Mileage figures are placeholders. Actual hauls would change the distant dairy result most.

## Quality and risk checks

- **Aflatoxin:** untested. Test before any feed or food sale.
- **Crude fiber and moisture:** not entered. Feed outlets need crude fiber below 15% [wcngg2022]. For the clean-and-recover option, the cleaned hulls must still meet that standard.
- **Equipment access:** clean-and-recover needs cleaning and kernel-recovery equipment.
- **Distant dairy:** needs long-haul truck or rail. Rail to Texas has precedent, but the premium isn't guaranteed [farmprogress_low].

## Assumptions and sources

Every result is tagged "placeholder," because each depends on at least one made-up input, such as mileage or processing cost. Sourced inputs are the dairy price range, the hauling rate, and the fiber standard.

- [abc_food2025] Almond Board of California, "Unlocking New Value: Commercializing Almond Hulls as Food Ingredients": https://www.almonds.org/almond-industry/industry-news/unlocking-new-value-commercializing-almond-hulls-food-ingredients
- [farmprogress_low] Farm Progress, "Almond hulls – Low prices call for expanded markets": https://www.farmprogress.com/tree-nuts/almond-hulls-low-prices-call-for-expanded-markets
- [giannini2026] UC Giannini Foundation, "Almond Shell Circularity in California's Bioeconomy" (2026): https://s.giannini.ucop.edu/uploads/pub/2026/06/26/v29n5_3_mg7Nqvg.pdf
- [gras2026] AgInfo, "Unlocking New Uses for Almond Hulls": https://www.aginfo.net/report/65481/32/Unlocking-New-Uses-for-Almond-Hulls
- [wcngg2022] WCNGG, "Almond Hull Prices are a Bright Spot" (2022): https://wcngg.com/2022/04/18/almond-hull-prices-are-a-bright-spot-for-the-almond-industry/

These are estimates. Confirm prices with buyer quotes and test the material's quality before deciding.

## Recommendation

Do not count on the local dairy route for this lot as it stands. The hulls test at 16% crude fiber, and the feed standard calls for below 15% [wcngg2022]. That makes all four feed options ineligible, including the baseline. The local dairy figure ($85 per ton expected, $85,000 for the lot) is only a reference point.

Of the eligible options with a price, the best is **bioenergy feedstock**, at $17 per ton expected ($17,000 total). Compost or soil amendment is close behind at $16 per ton ($16,000). Both are far below the dairy reference, and both rest entirely on placeholder values. Treat them as fallbacks, not firm plans.

The most useful next step is to retest fiber and test for aflatoxin. If a retest or a cleaning step brings fiber below 15%, the feed routes may open up.

## How the options compare

Net is per ton delivered, after processing and hauling. Totals are for 1,000 tons.

| Option | Eligible | Net per ton (expected) | Total | Versus dairy reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bioenergy | Yes | $17 | $17,000 | -$68,000 |
| Compost/soil | Yes | $16 | $16,000 | -$69,000 |
| Clean, recover kernels, dairy | No (fiber) | $98 | $98,000 | +$13,000 |
| Local dairy (baseline) | No (fiber) | $85 | $85,000 | reference |
| Distant dairy | No (fiber) | $56 | $56,000 | -$29,000 |
| Food ingredient | Needs quote | none | none | none |

The food ingredient option has no price, so it can't be recommended. Its buyer would need to pay $175 per ton to match the local dairy reference.

## What could change the answer

- **Fiber result.** This is the biggest factor. Feed outlets are blocked at 16%. Cleaning is listed as a possible route, but its requirement is that cleaned hulls end up below 15%. That is not shown here.
- **Dairy price swings.** Prices have ranged from about a $60 slump to $130 per ton [farmprogress_low, wcngg2022]. The recent range is $76–$106 [giannini2026].
- **Food buyer quote.** A quote of $175 per ton or more would match the dairy reference.
- **Placeholder inputs.** Bioenergy and compost prices, processing costs and distances are all placeholders, so those two results could move a lot.

## Quality and risk checks

- Crude fiber is 16%, so all feed outlets fail the standard [wcngg2022].
- Aflatoxin is untested. Test before any feed or food sale.
- Moisture is not entered.
- About 97% of hulls already go to dairy rations, so buyers have leverage [farmprogress_low].
- Recovered kernels may grade lower than standard kernels. This is a general caution, not from a source.
- Distant dairy: freight can erase the price premium, and the premium is not guaranteed [farmprogress_low].

## Assumptions and sources

**Sourced:** the hauling rate ($0.30 per ton-mile, within the illustrative range in [giannini2026]), the dairy price range, the fiber standard, and the price history.

**Placeholder:** all bioenergy and compost values, most distances, the cleaning cost, the recovered-kernel value, and the distant-dairy and food prices. Results for every outlet are therefore placeholder-tier.

Sources:

- [gras2026] AgInfo, "Unlocking New Uses for Almond Hulls": https://www.aginfo.net/report/65481/32/Unlocking-New-Uses-for-Almond-Hulls
- [wcngg2022] WCNGG, "Almond Hull Prices are a Bright Spot" (2022): https://wcngg.com/2022/04/18/almond-hull-prices-are-a-bright-spot-for-the-almond-industry/

These are estimates. Confirm prices with buyer quotes and test the material's quality before deciding.

judge_issues: Decision clarity: the Recommendation names two options and acts on neither. It says of the food ingredient "I would not act on it yet" and calls clean-and-recover "the steadier, nearer-term step". It never states one action, such as getting a toll-cleaning or equipment quote and a food-buyer quote while keeping the local dairy sale. A manager cannot tell whether to switch, invest in cleaning, or stay with the baseline.

"The steadier, nearer-term step" is not supported by the payload. Clean-and-recover has status "emerging". Its cleaning cost and kernel value are placeholders. Its net range ($80–$116) is wider than the baseline's ($70–$100). Calling it "steadier" overstates confidence.

"Before selling anywhere, test for aflatoxin" is broader than the payload. The aflatoxin flag applies only to the food, clean-and-recover, local dairy and distant dairy options. Bioenergy and compost have no flags.

Clean-and-recover placeholders are listed incompletely in the Recommendation. It says "Its kernel value and cleaning cost are placeholders" but leaves out that its distance (miles) is also a placeholder.
The payload risk "Cleaning cost is a demo placeholder; get an equipment or toll-cleaning quote" is not turned into a next step, although this cost drives the recommended option's edge.

The payload requirement that cleaned hulls must still meet the feed standard (crude fiber below 15%) is not tied to the clean-and-recover option. The report states the standard only generally for feed outlets.
"The report treats them as eligible, but that is unconfirmed until you test" is an awkward self-reference. Plainer: "These options assume your hulls meet the standard; test to confirm."

Before you sell, test for aflatoxin. It has not been tested, and the dairy and every feed or food route need that test.

## How the options compare

| Option | Expected net per ton | Expected total | Versus dairy (total) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local dairy (baseline) | $85 | $85,000 | – |
| Clean, recover kernels, sell to dairy | $75 | $75,000 | -$10,000 |
| Distant dairy market | $56 | $56,000 | -$29,000 |
| Bioenergy | $17 | $17,000 | -$68,000 |
| Compost or soil | $16 | $16,000 | -$69,000 |
| Hull powder food ingredient | no price | – | – |

- **Distant dairy:** The higher price ($116–$146 per ton) is a placeholder, and $75 per ton of freight eats the premium. The buyer would need to pay $160 per ton to match the local dairy.
- **Bioenergy and compost:** All values are placeholders, and both fall far behind. Bioenergy would need $103 per ton and compost $99 per ton to match the baseline.

## What could change the answer

- **Local price swings.** Hull prices have ranged from about $60 per ton in a slump to $130 per ton [farmprogress_low, wcngg2022]. A drop would hurt, but the cleaning option would drop with it, since its price follows the dairy's.
- **A real quote from a distant buyer.** The distant-dairy price is a placeholder. A firm quote of $160 per ton or more, after the freight, would put it level with the dairy.

- **Kernel grade.** Recovered kernels may grade lower than standard kernels. This is a general caution, not from a cited source.
- **Long-haul logistics.** Rail shipments to Texas have precedent, but a premium is not guaranteed [farmprogress_low].

**Placeholders:** all hauling distances, the cleaning cost, and every price for the distant dairy, bioenergy, compost and food routes. The kernel value is user-entered. The ranking of the lower options depends on these placeholders.

- **Buyer leverage.** About 97% of hulls already go to dairy rations, so buyers have the upper hand [farmprogress_low].
- **Haul distance.** Miles are placeholders. Your $0.60 per ton-mile haul rate is your own figure, and it is higher than the illustrative $0.20–$0.40 in the Giannini source [giannini2026]. It hurts distant options most.

## Recommendation

Clean the hulls, recover the kernels, then sell to the local dairy. It nets about $94 per ton, or about $112,980 for the 1,200 tons. That is $8 per ton (about $9,060 total) more than selling straight to the local dairy, which nets about $87 per ton, or $103,920 in total.

This edge is small and rests on user-entered numbers. The cleaning cost ($12 per ton) and the value of the recovered kernels ($17 to $22 per ton) are both user figures, not sourced. Get a cleaning quote and a kernel buyer's price before committing. If the quotes come in worse, selling to the local dairy is a sound fallback.

| Local dairy (baseline) | $87 | $103,920 | none |

| Food ingredient powder | $53 | $63,600 | -$40,320 |
| Compost or soil | $17 | $19,800 | -$84,120 |
| Bioenergy | $14 | $16,200 | -$87,720 |

The distant dairy pays $138 per ton, but hauling 240 miles costs $72 per ton and eats the premium. It would need about $159 per ton to match the baseline. The food ingredient route would need about $184, and it has no public market price [gras2026]. Compost and bioenergy would need about $98 and $105, far above the $28 and $32 assumed.

scenarios.report:
## Recommendation

Keep sending the pomace to cattle feed unless a food-ingredient buyer gives you a firm quote. Every option here loses money on expected terms. The baseline, wet pomace to dairy/beef feed, loses the least among the options that rest on firm routes: an expected -$13 per ton, or -$3,900 on 300 tons.

The ingredients route (seed oil, polyphenol extract, marc powder) ranks first, at an expected -$4.50 per ton (-$1,350 total). That is only $8.50 per ton better than the baseline. Its range runs from -$15,000 to +$12,300, so it could easily come out worse. All of these figures are placeholder-based (see below), so I would not switch on this margin alone.

## How the options compare

Net is the expected money left per ton of pomace after processing and hauling. Negative means you pay.

| Option | Net per ton | Total (300 t) | vs. baseline per ton |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ingredients (seed oil, extracts) | -$4.50 | -$1,350 | +$8.50 |
| **Wet feed (baseline)** | -$13 | -$3,900 | 0 |
| Distillation and tartrate | -$14 | -$4,200 | -$1 |
| Dried feed | -$20.05 | -$6,015 | -$7.05 |
| Compost | -$26 | -$7,800 | -$13 |
| Biogas digestion | -$26.50 | -$7,950 | -$13.50 |
| Biochar | -$102 | -$30,600 | -$89 |

To match the baseline, a buyer would need to pay this much per ton of product: ingredients $6.50, distillation $11, dried feed about $93, biochar $84. Compost and biogas would match it at a gate fee of $7 and $4 per ton respectively (a negative price, meaning you pay that much or less).

## What could change the answer

- **Ingredient buyer quote.** Few California buyers exist and volumes are small, so a firm price is the biggest swing factor.
- **Feed price.** The baseline price range is $0 to $10 per ton. A winery executive said the pomace needs to bring more than $10 a ton to beat cattle feed [grape_pressdemocrat2015].
- **Gate fees.** California green-waste gate fees run about $35–115 per ton, and wet fruit residues may cost more [calrecycle_stanislaus_fees_2026]. That is well above the compost and biogas fees assumed here, so those two could look worse.
- **Distance.** Feed assumes 60 miles one way, and a closer or farther buyer shifts the haul cost.

## Quality and risk checks

- All seven options passed the quality checks, and none is flagged.
- Feed pomace must be delivered within one to two days of pressing [grape_palatepress]. Digestibility is poor (about 30%), which caps its value. Coastal wineries may have no nearby dairy [both_agproud_byproducts]. Pesticide and sulfite residue limits are not sourced.
- Ingredients need pomace dried or separated before it molds. The status of the polyphenol buyer is unverified (2016 source) [grape_nutraingredients_polyphenolics].
- Distillation needs a permit, and white pomace must be fermented first.
- The Napa digester has no start date [grape_biocycle_napa_ad].
- Compost needs a carbon source such as rice hulls [grape_wastedive_napa].
- Fertilizer value of the nutrients is not counted in any net figure.

## Assumptions and sources

Only the haul rate ($0.30 per ton-mile) is sourced. Prices, processing costs, miles and coproduct values are placeholders, so every result depends on placeholder values. Treat the ranking as a guide to what to quote, not as a forecast.

Sources:
- [grape_pressdemocrat2015] Sonoma County winemakers find uses for pomace (Press Democrat, 2015): https://www.pressdemocrat.com/lifestyle/4009143-181/sonoma-county-winemakers-find-uses?page=0
- [grape_palatepress] Pomace to Pours, Preservatives, and Power (Palate Press): https://www.palatepress.com/pomace-to-pours-preservatives-and-power-dealing-with-winery-waste/
- [both_agproud_byproducts] The vital role of byproduct use in California dairy feed rations: https://agproud.com/topics/feed-nutrition/the-vital-role-of-byproduct-use-in-california-dairy-feed-rations
- [grape_nutraingredients_polyphenolics] Polyphenolics delves into sports nutrition (NutraIngredients, 2016): https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2016/10/19/Polyphenolics-delves-into-sports-nutrition-with-its-grape-seed-extracts/
- [grape_biocycle_napa_ad] Napa anaerobic digestion + composting project (BioCycle, April 2026): https://www.biocycle.net/?p=57005
- [grape_wastedive_napa] Napa compost / Upper Valley grape pomace (Waste Dive): https://www.wastedive.com/news/napa-compost-upper-valley-grape-pomace-wine-country/634301/

These are estimates. Confirm prices with buyer quotes and test the material's quality before deciding.

scenarios.report:
## Recommendation

Keep selling pressed or ensiled peel wet to dairies and cattle feeders for now. At the placeholder numbers, the lot costs about $12,500 in total (a loss of $12/ton at the midpoint, range $5,000 to $20,000). None of the three options that beat this do so with confidence, and every figure here depends on placeholder values.

Two options look slightly better on paper:
- **Recover d-limonene (peel oil), residue to feed:** about $12,000 better than the baseline, or about $500 lost in total. Its price follows the baseline price, so its edge comes only from the oil coproduct value. That value rests on a 2012 trade article [orange_limonene_price] and is a demo number.
- **Dry into pellets:** about $3,610 better, but still a loss of about $8,890 in total.

I would get a quote on limonene recovery before switching. Don't switch on these numbers alone.

## How the options compare

Per ton of peel, expected net (midpoint):

| Option | Net per ton | Total, 1,000 tons | vs. baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Limonene recovery | -$0.50 | -$500 | +$12,000 |
| Dry into pellets | -$8.89 | -$8,890 | +$3,610 |
| **Baseline: wet to cattle feeders** | -$12.50 | -$12,500 | 0 |
| Anaerobic digestion | -$56.50 | -$56,500 | -$44,000 |
| Compost | -$77.50 | -$77,500 | -$65,000 |
| Pectin/fiber | needs quote | n/a | n/a |
| Ethanol | needs quote | n/a | n/a |

Pectin/fiber and ethanol have no price, so I can't recommend them. To match the baseline, a pectin buyer would need to pay $152.50 per ton of product, and an ethanol buyer $42.50. Pellet buyers would need to pay $159.30 per ton of pellets to match the baseline, against a placeholder range of $150 to $200.

Digestion and compost would match the baseline only if the fee became a small payment to you ($1.50 and $2.50 per ton, respectively). Fertilizer value is shown for these two but is not counted in the net.

## What could change the answer

- **Limonene price:** the oil coproduct is the whole advantage, and that price swings with citrus crop size [orange_limonene_price].
- **Pellet price:** the range of $150 to $200 per ton of pellets is a placeholder. Pellet net stays negative even at the high end.
- **Buyer quotes:** the baseline price range runs from paying $5 to receiving $10 per ton, so the real buyer terms matter a lot.
- **Compost gate fees:** California green-waste fees run about $35 to $115 per ton, and wet fruit may cost more [calrecycle_stanislaus_fees_2026].
- **Distance:** hauling is $0.30 per ton-mile (sourced); the miles are placeholders.

## Quality and risk checks

- All options are eligible and none has a quality flag. Moisture for the lot was not entered.
- **Baseline:** raw peel spoils, and ensiling takes about a month. Press liquor is about a third of peel weight and needs wastewater handling. One or two firms handle most juice-plant peel [orange_vincent_waste][orange_rwqcb_tipton]. Dairy inclusion should stay below about 20% of ration dry matter [orange_feedipedia].
- **Limonene recovery:** needs vapor recovery, or the oil is lost in drying.
- **Pellets:** need an air permit, and California dryers were shut down for environmental reasons [orange_vincent_waste].
- **Digestion and compost:** few California sites take juice-plant peel, and compost needs bulking material.
- **Pectin:** no operating US peel buyer was found, and wash-water disposal ended California washing [orange_vincent_pectin].
- **Ethanol:** no California peel-ethanol plant was found, and limonene must be removed first.

## Assumptions and sources

**Sourced:** the haul rate. Digestion and compost miles are also sourced. Yields cited include 32.8% pectin and 0.495 g ethanol per g of sugar [team_yields_2026].
**Placeholder:** all prices, processing costs, and the other distances, so every net result here is a placeholder.

Sources:
- [ca_agproud_byproducts] Ag Proud, byproduct use in California dairy rations: https://www.agproud.com/articles/54889-the-vital-role-of-byproduct-use-in-california-dairy-feed-rations
- [ca_anaergia] Anaergia, SB 1383 compliance: https://www.anaergia.com/sb-1383-compliance-organic-waste-to-renewable-fuel-and-fertilizer
- [ca_biocycle_midvalley] BioCycle, Mid Valley Disposal, Kerman: https://www.biocycle.net/?p=27055
- [orange_ad_ensiling] Orange peel ensiling for digestion: https://agris.fao.org/search/en/records/65e013d20f3e94b9e5deff8e
- [orange_ad_limonene] Ruiz Fuertes & Flotats 2016: https://agris.fao.org/search/en/records/6748865e7625988a371d02d4
- [orange_ars_cows] USDA ARS, peel as cattle feed: https://agresearchmag.ars.usda.gov/2011/nov/cows
- [orange_feedipedia] Feedipedia, dried citrus pulp: https://www.feedipedia.org/Node/680
- [orange_limonene_price] Asphalt Pro, d-limonene costs: https://theasphaltpro.com/?p=7248
- [orange_rwqcb_tipton] Water Board Order R5-2015-0135: https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/rwqcb5/board_decisions/adopted_orders/tulare/r5-2015-0135.pdf
- [orange_vincent_pectin] Vincent Corp, pectin peel: https://vincentcorp.com/content/pectin-peel
- [orange_vincent_waste] Vincent Corp, citrus waste disposal: https://vincentcorp.com/content/citrus-waste-disposal
- [team_yields_2026] BioCycle team yield review (no link yet)
- [calrecycle_stanislaus_fees_2026] cited in the payload without a listed title or URL.

These are estimates. Confirm prices with buyer quotes and test the material's quality before deciding.
